"I am bringing the gods incense and natron.
I want to expel the bad smell from your mouth.
Therefore I come in order to expel the evil in your hearts.
With this I remove the Evil, Isfet, which clings to you.
With this I bring you Good.
I present Justice, Maat, to you......""

before: breton.0028.desc:0 "I am almost finished with the Tro Breizh, for I now arrive in Vannes, the seventh and last stop on this pilgrimage. It is, despite being a very ancient settlement - dating to before the Roman Emperors, learned men tell me - a very joyous and exciting place as well. I found, for example, much amusement in the comically puffy, ugly granite statues the locals dub "Vannes and his Wife." Some of the locals also explained the lore of the ancient large stones that dot the area.\n\nBut this is a time for religion, not mirth. I reflect on the Saint of Vannes, Saint Patern. They say this Saint was a contemporary of the mighty King Arthur, the great Briton hero; he tamed the king's avarice and humbled the monarch according to the legends. At any rate, I too, must practice the virtues. This is why I went on this pilgrimage after all."

before: RICE_bamian_repair_shahr_e_zohak_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Shahr-e Zohak is one of the most impressive fortifications ever built in Afghanistan; one scholar even called it the "Afghan Krak des Chevaliers." It was occupied by successive groups, such as the Hephthalites, Ghaznavids, Ghurids, and Timurids. Zohak is an evil figure in Persian mythology, and though it is uncertain why the fortress is named after him, he is said to be the ancestor of the nearby Ghurids. A legend has it that the fortress city was destroyed by Genghis Khan, and all its inhabitants massacred as revenge for his grandson's death when it was besieged."

before: RICE_tarim_basin_compile_the_turkic_dictionary_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! before: RICE_galicia_pray_to_santiago_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! As an important holy figure in medieval Iberian Christendom, Saint James (or Santiago) symbolized different things depending on contemporary politics and culture. For example, his earlier portrayal as James the Pilgrim was increasingly supplanted by his role as James the Warrior or the Moor-Slayer in the late medieval period. In the New World, he was initially the "Indian Slayer" during the conquest of the Americas, but later became the "Spaniard Slayer" to revolutionaries in Latin America fighting Spanish rule in the 1800s."

before: RICE_bozo_mud_masons_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Mudbricks have been a conspicuous part of buildings in West Africa for centuries, with the Mosque of Djenne as perhaps the most famous example of this style of architecture. Mud masons are respected throughout the region for their practical, spiritual, and sorcerous knowledge, as construction requires not only creating the building, but also the use of spells and incantations to bless the site and exorcise evil spirits. For example, many mud masons in the city of Jenne are of the Bozo ethnicity, and are well-versed in Islamic Quranic verses and what they refer to as #italic bai bibi#!, or "African secrets," the details of which they seldom disclose to outsiders."

before: RICE_bozo_move_jenne_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Jenne-Jeno ("Old Jenne"), the original site of Jenne, was a major urban center in present-day Mali but was abandoned sometime in the medieval period. According to legend, this move happened when the Soninke migrated to the region; they tried to establish a town near the original site settled by the Bozo, but were met with various natural disasters. They were only able to found the city after an oracle told them to sacrifice a virgin girl by burying her alive in the city walls. The tomb of this girl, known as Tapama Djenepo (i.e. "Tapama, the Martyr of Djenne"), still stands in modern Jenne."

before:
bao.0001.desc:0 "My soldiers bring forth two young black-costumed men whom they arrested outside my residence.

"This low-born rabble was found sleeping in a dried ditch, my [ROOT.Char.GetLadyLord]," one of my soldiers says when asked who they are. "They say they are church musicians, but they were acting suspiciously, and it is clear they are highway robbers who are using your property without permission."

Another soldier interjects, "While I do agree they are acting suspiciously, we shouldn't be too hasty to make any judgment.

The first soldier ignores the other's comment, and says, "They are highwaymen, whether you like it or not, so I suggest we give them a swift exemplary punishment for trespassing.""

Another soldier interjects, "While I do agree they are acting suspiciously, we shouldn't be too hasty to make any judgment.

The first soldier ignores the other's comment, and says, "They are highwaymen, whether you like it or not, so I suggest we give them a swift exemplary punishment for trespassing.""

before: bao.0001.info:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Up until the mid XXth century, costumes were the most reliable way to tell the social status of a stranger; in Brittany, black costumes were un-embroided costumes for the poorest of the poor. The "Sonerien Du" or "Black Musicians" were traveling singers and musicians paid mostly in food and drink, who went from church to church, mass to mass, and wedding to wedding to do their trade. They had the reputation of playing "hep diskrog" or "restlessly" and according to local superstition, a Breton wedding could only end when the musician was too drunk to play. They often were seen as troublemakers by the Gendarmes and the upper stratas of Breton society.\n The actual "Sonerien Du" legend which is the reference for the event is the legend of the Bro Vigouden (Barony of Kemper) where two black-coated musicians were unjustly punished around 1790 in Pont-'n-Abad (Pont-l'-Abbé in French) and sentenced to death for sleeping dead drunk in the roadside, either because they were mistaken for highway robbers or as the result of the corruption of the local aristocracy. Their bodies were exposed on spikes for everyone to see. Because this event coincided with (unverified) plague outbreaks, people held them as martyrs, and would touch the bodies, believing it would grant plague immunity."

Our "agreements" with them have not been working in our favor, and even though many are also respectable merchants, can we really trust them when they are no less greedier than the average charlatan and bandit?

I have thus sent out an order to immediately renege on any of our agreements with pirate groups in the [GetGeographicalRegion('RICE_indian_ocean_region').GetName]. before: rice_vajrayana_canon_doctrine_desc:0 "The Tantric Canon is the collection of Buddhist texts accepted by the so-called esoteric schools of Buddhism, such as Tibetan Vajrayana and sects influenced by them. The Tibetan Canon for example consists of the Kangyur ("Translation of the Word") and Tengyur ("Translation of Treatises"). These canons include Mahayana texts, as well as texts from early schools of Buddhism that are not part of or were discarded from the Pali Canon."

before:
khwarezm.0014.desc:0 "The citadel of Al-Fir in [kath.GetNameNoTier] has stood proudly for many years. This beautiful and mighty fortress can be seen for miles and miles, and served as a symbol of the local rulers' might and prestige. Alas, it also happens to be located next to the Amu Darya or Oxus River, nicknamed the "Mad River" due to its tendency to change course or overflood erratically.

Over the years, the citadel has managed to withstand assault after assault by the waters of the Oxus, but its defenses have gradually worn out. Though the main structure of the fortress is still standing, it is partly ruined, and local authorities have deemed it no longer safe to use on a large scale, and the administration has relocated to other structures in town.

Still, at least the citadel remains standing. Even if it is no longer in frequent use, it will surely continue to inspire and embolden the inhabitants nearby."

before:
game_concept_mahavihara_desc:0 "The Mahavihara, alongside the [abhayagiri|E] and [jetavana|E], are one of the three major [RICE_sri_lanka_monasteries|E] in the [RICE_sri_lanka_struggle|E], or its Buddhist community. In-game, the Mahavihara are represented by an orange icon: @RICE_mahavihara_icon!.

You can raise or lower the [RICE_sri_lanka_prominence|E] of the Mahavihara through different [decisions|E], [activities|E], and so on, especially if you have the [GetTrait('RICE_mahavihara_trait').GetName( GetNullCharacter )] [trait|E], which can be gained by taking the [decision|E] to $RICE_sri_lanka_choose_monastic_sect$. Keep this in mind if you wish to end the [struggle|E] in [RICE_sri_lanka_short|E].

Historically, the Mahavihara were the more 'traditionalist' monastery or sect of ancient and medieval Sri Lankan Buddhism. They were typically skeptical or dismissive of what they saw as heterodox ideas from India. According to traditional chronicles, they were the ones who "won" out in the end against the other monasteries."

before: RICE_sri_lanka_worship_local_deities_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! For centuries, the people of Sri Lanka have worshipped a variety of shared deities, regardless of whether they are Buddhist or Hindu, or Sinhala, Tamil, or Vedda. Many of these deities were syncretized forms of Hindu, Buddhist, and indigenous religious figures, known by different names from different communities and often worshipped in a manner distinct from mainland India. Some were even historical Sri Lankan figures like kings turned into deities. For the island's Buddhists, while the Buddha is considered superior to these "lesser" deities, the latter are often invoked for more worldly concerns."

before:

We pray to remind ourselves about the importance of the Three Jewels – the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha – as we make offerings where the Dharmadhatu lays. I reflect on the Dharmadhatu while doing so.

The text itself expounds on the #italic Trikaya#! or "three bodies" teaching on the nature of reality and Buddhahood, found in the [GetDoctrineType('rice_mahayana_canon_doctrine').GetBaseName]. Some detractors criticize the Dharmadhatu’s teachings as unorthodox, even heretical, but others believe its spiritual ideas can help and guide all, and so it is worthy of veneration."

before: RICE_sicily_second_pavia_decision_desc:0 "After the fall of the Kingdom of the Lombards, and the loss of their glorious capital, Pavia, the Lombards' heirs have wandered and survived in southern Italy. before: RICE_sicily_second_pavia_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Pavia was the capital of the Lombard Kingdom that dominated Italy from the 6th to 8th centuries, until its defeat by the Carolingian Franks. Lombard successor states emerged in southern Italy, and Benevento, a major center of Lombard power there, was even known as a "second Pavia" due to its prosperity and prominence. Ironically, these same Lombard polities were often dominated by the Franks to the north. The Lombards in the south would remain a distinct identity up until the era of Norman Sicily in the 12th and 13th centuries."
after: RICE_sicily_second_pavia_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Pavia was the capital of the Lombard Kingdom that dominated Italy from the 6th to 8th centuries, until its defeat by the Carolingian Franks. Lombard successor states emerged in southern Italy, and Benevento, a major center of Lombard power there, was even known as a \"second Pavia\" due to its prosperity and prominence. Ironically, these same Lombard polities were often dominated by the Franks to the north. The Lombards in the south would remain a distinct identity up until the era of Norman Sicily in the 12th and 13th centuries."

before: RICE_sicily_byzantine_syracuse_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Syracuse was one of the great cities of the ancient Mediterranean; Cicero, for instance, described it as "the greatest Greek city and the most beautiful of them all." It retained its importance during the early Byzantine period, particularly after the empire's loss of its African territories; it even briefly served as the capital of the empire from 663-669 CE. With the Muslim conquest of Sicily, including the fall of Syracuse in 878, the island's center moved to Palermo, and while Syracuse still remained a major city on the island, it never regained its former preeminent status."
after: RICE_sicily_byzantine_syracuse_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! before: RICE_sicily_catania_elephant_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! #italic U Liotru#! is a famous elephant statue in the city of Catania. The name is a corruption of Heliodorus, a legendary 8th century necromancer and sorcerer who either brought the statue to life, or transformed into it himself, before he was defeated by Saint Leo of Catania. Though the legend is of dubious historicity, the city has been associated with the statue for centuries; the Arabs called Catania the "city of the Elephant," and the geographer al-Idrisi, who worked at the court of King Roger II of Sicily, believed the statue was made by the Carthaginians or Romans and that the Catanese considered the statue to be magical and able to protect them from Mount Etna's eruptions. In 1239, the statue was chosen to be the city's symbol. After an earthquake, it was repurposed into a fountain in 1737."

In 1239, the statue was chosen to be the city's symbol. After an earthquake, it was repurposed into a fountain in 1737."

before: sicily.0001.desc:0 ""Sicily was the first of our provinces; Sicily first taught our ancestors how glorious it could be to rule other peoples." So said the great Roman Cicero, long before Rome declined in the West.\n\nSicily, crucible of the Mediterranean, is now a wild frontier where three worlds meet: Islam, Byzantium, and the Latin West. Many covet Sicily and its abundance, but would-be conquerors and settlers often find behind this paradise is a liminal land where the boundaries between culture, faith, and loyalty can be very blurry."

before: activity_RICE_yazidi_tawus_geran_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Tawûs Gêran, the "Touring of Tawûs," is a Yazidi ceremony that involves the parading of a #italic sanjak#!, a standard of Melek Taus (the Peacock Angel). #italic Qewals#!, who are hereditary performers of Yazidi religious hymns, would thus bring with them the #italic sanjak#! as they travel to different Yazidi villages, as long as it is a time of peace adn when they are certain the roads are safe. before:
yorkshire.0106.desc:0 "I am reflecting over the life and times of Alcuin, that famous scholar and monk from York and who became an important intellectual of Charlemagne’s court. He trained many important thinkers of his era, and I feel a little sense of pride at the thought that I rule territories not too far from where he was born and grew up in. Two of his famous sayings, I recall, include:

"Remember to care for the soul more than the body, since the former remains, the latter perishes."

"And do not listen to those who keep saying, 'The voice of the people is the voice of God', because the tumult of the crowd is always close to madness.""

before: RICE_south_ethiopia_sidama_groves_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! The Sidama people have traditionally maintained and worshipped at sacred trees or groves regardless of religion. before: RICE_khwarezm_the_mad_river_desc:0 "The Amu Darya or Oxus is one of the great rivers of the world. Though its fertile banks contribute to the prosperity of the surrounding regions, it is also called the "Mad River," for it often shifts its course and overfloods – sometimes gradually, sometimes suddenly – particularly along the [GetGeographicalRegion('RICE_lower_oxus_region').GetName]. Locals frequently relocate entire settlements, and foreigners scornfully remark on the filthy conditions in these otherwise prosperous cities due to the flooding."

before:
khwarezm.0014.desc:0 "The citadel of Al-Fir in [kath.GetNameNoTier] has stood proudly for many years. This beautiful and mighty fortress can be seen for miles and miles, and served as a symbol of the local rulers' might and prestige. Alas, it also happens to be located next to the Amu Darya or Oxus River, nicknamed the "Mad River" due to its tendency to change course or overflood erratically.

Over the years, the citadel has managed to withstand assault after assault by the waters of the Oxus, but its defenses have gradually worn out. Though the main structure of the fortress is still standing, it is partly ruined, and local authorities have deemed it no longer safe to use on a large scale, and the administration has relocated to other structures in town.

Still, at least the citadel remains standing. Even if it is no longer in frequent use, it will surely continue to inspire and embolden the inhabitants nearby."

before: RICE_lesbos_fortify_aegean_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Since ancient times, the [GetGeographicalRegion('RICE_aegean_region').GetNameNoTooltip] has attracted frequent piracy, maritime raids, and naval warfare due to its strategic geographical location. before:
lesbos.0051.desc:0 "We have tolerated the presence of pirates in my territories for far too long. Our "agreements" with them have not been working in our favor, and even though many are also respectable merchants, can we really trust them when they are no less greedier than the average charlatan and bandit?

I have thus sent out an order to immediately renege on any of our agreements with pirate groups in the [GetGeographicalRegion('RICE_mediterranean_region').GetName]. They will no longer be afforded legal protections nor the ability to set up their base of operations in my territories by working with us, because they no longer work #italic for#! us.

I have ordered my troops to make sure these pirates comply with our commands. We can only hope they leave peaceably...."

before:
game_concept_mahavihara_desc:0 "The Mahavihara, alongside the [abhayagiri|E] and [jetavana|E], are one of the three major [RICE_sri_lanka_monasteries|E] in the [RICE_sri_lanka_struggle|E], or its Buddhist community. In-game, the Mahavihara are represented by an orange icon: @RICE_mahavihara_icon!.

You can raise or lower the [RICE_sri_lanka_prominence|E] of the Mahavihara through different [decisions|E], [activities|E], and so on, especially if you have the [GetTrait('RICE_mahavihara_trait').GetName( GetNullCharacter )] [trait|E], which can be gained by taking the [decision|E] to $RICE_sri_lanka_choose_monastic_sect$. Keep this in mind if you wish to end the [struggle|E] in [RICE_sri_lanka_short|E].

Historically, the Mahavihara were the more 'traditionalist' monastery or sect of ancient and medieval Sri Lankan Buddhism. They were typically skeptical or dismissive of what they saw as heterodox ideas from India. According to traditional chronicles, they were the ones who "won" out in the end against the other monasteries."

before: RICE_sri_lanka_worship_local_deities_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! For centuries, the people of Sri Lanka have worshipped a variety of shared deities, regardless of whether they are Buddhist or Hindu, or Sinhala, Tamil, or Vedda. Many of these deities were syncretized forms of Hindu, Buddhist, and indigenous religious figures, known by different names from different communities and often worshipped in a manner distinct from mainland India. Some were even historical Sri Lankan figures like kings turned into deities. For the island's Buddhists, while the Buddha is considered superior to these "lesser" deities, the latter are often invoked for more worldly concerns."

before:
sri_lanka.0103.desc.dharmadhatu:0 "The chanting of prayers ring in the air, and the march of people and elephants, as the procession and worship ceremony begins.

We pray to remind ourselves about the importance of the Three Jewels – the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha – as we make offerings where the Dharmadhatu lays. I reflect on the Dharmadhatu while doing so.

The text itself expounds on the #italic Trikaya#! or "three bodies" teaching on the nature of reality and Buddhahood, found in the [GetDoctrineType('rice_mahayana_canon_doctrine').GetBaseName]. Some detractors criticize the Dharmadhatu’s teachings as unorthodox, even heretical, but others believe its spiritual ideas can help and guide all, and so it is worthy of veneration."

before: RICE_sicily_second_pavia_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Pavia was the capital of the Lombard Kingdom that dominated Italy from the 6th to 8th centuries, until its defeat by the Carolingian Franks. Lombard successor states emerged in southern Italy, and Benevento, a major center of Lombard power there, was even known as a "second Pavia" due to its prosperity and prominence. Ironically, these same Lombard polities were often dominated by the Franks to the north. The Lombards in the south would remain a distinct identity up until the era of Norman Sicily in the 12th and 13th centuries."

before: RICE_sicily_byzantine_syracuse_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Syracuse was one of the great cities of the ancient Mediterranean; Cicero, for instance, described it as "the greatest Greek city and the most beautiful of them all." It retained its importance during the early Byzantine period, particularly after the empire's loss of its African territories; it even briefly served as the capital of the empire from 663-669 CE. With the Muslim conquest of Sicily, including the fall of Syracuse in 878, the island's center moved to Palermo, and while Syracuse still remained a major city on the island, it never regained its former preeminent status."

before: RICE_sicily_catania_elephant_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! #italic U Liotru#! is a famous elephant statue in the city of Catania. The name is a corruption of Heliodorus, a legendary 8th century necromancer and sorcerer who either brought the statue to life, or transformed into it himself, before he was defeated by Saint Leo of Catania. Though the legend is of dubious historicity, the city has been associated with the statue for centuries; the Arabs called Catania the "city of the Elephant," and the geographer al-Idrisi, who worked at the court of King Roger II of Sicily, believed the statue was made by the Carthaginians or Romans and that the Catanese considered the statue to be magical and able to protect them from Mount Etna's eruptions. In 1239, the statue was chosen to be the city's symbol. After an earthquake, it was repurposed into a fountain in 1737."

before: sicily.0001.desc:0 ""Sicily was the first of our provinces; Sicily first taught our ancestors how glorious it could be to rule other peoples." So said the great Roman Cicero, long before Rome declined in the West.\n\nSicily, crucible of the Mediterranean, is now a wild frontier where three worlds meet: Islam, Byzantium, and the Latin West. Many covet Sicily and its abundance, but would-be conquerors and settlers often find behind this paradise is a liminal land where the boundaries between culture, faith, and loyalty can be very blurry."

before:
yorkshire.0106.desc:0 "I am reflecting over the life and times of Alcuin, that famous scholar and monk from York and who became an important intellectual of Charlemagne’s court. He trained many important thinkers of his era, and I feel a little sense of pride at the thought that I rule territories not too far from where he was born and grew up in. Two of his famous sayings, I recall, include:

"Remember to care for the soul more than the body, since the former remains, the latter perishes."

"And do not listen to those who keep saying, 'The voice of the people is the voice of God', because the tumult of the crowd is always close to madness.""

The lands along the so-called "Silk Roads" have been home to a blend of many ethnicities, religions, and cultures, then and now. before: RICE_tarim_basin_compile_the_turkic_dictionary_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Diwan Lughat al-Turk, or "Compendium of the Languages of the Turks," is the magnum opus of Mahmud al-Kashgari, a Karakhanid scholar who was possibly distantly related to the ruling Karakhanid clan. Written in 1072-1074 CE, it was intended for use by the Caliphs of Baghdad who were under Seljuk domination. The book was not only a mere dictionary, as it also included a map of the world from Japan to Egypt, various notes on history and geography, and examples of old Turkic poetry. As the first Turkic dictionary, it is a valuable historical resource."

Due to various historical and present trends, though minor tensions surface from time to time, the Jews have become an accepted part of Granadan society and are probably here to stay.\n\n#italic While this [county_modifier|E] is active, [rulers|E] of the [county|E] of Granada may occasionally receive talented Jewish courtiers to serve in their court.#!"

before: RICE_granada_alhambra_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! The Alhambra (from Arabic #italic Al-Hamra#!, meaning "the Red One") was a palace and fortress complex of the Nasrid dynasty of Granada, and the epitome of medieval Moorish architecture. As a self-contained city, it had its own amenities likes bathhouses and mosques, and was continually expanded by the Nasrids from the 13th to 15th centuries. A striking element of the Alhambra is how many of its walls, columns, fountains, and other surfaces are covered in Quranic verses or poetry from poets of the time, writen in Arabic calligraphy."

before:
granada.0014.desc:0 "I was sleeping at my manor in [granada.GetNameNoTier] when my guards woke me late at night - chaos has erupted in the city's streets!

Apparently, a false rumor had spread earlier today that the Jewish official [yusuf.GetFullName] and other Jews had defected to an enemy ruler, opened the city gates, and killed me. Thanks to recent, rising anti-Jewish sentiment, a mob quickly formed to "protect" the city. Obviously, I’m alive and [granada.GetNameNoTierNoTooltip] is safe.

Before I know it, [yusuf.GetFirstName] arrives in a panic, begging for help. Moments later, the mob storms my palace, screaming how they will kill the "traitor" [yusuf.GetFirstName] before going for his fellow Jews next. I rush to meet the mob to reassure them that I am fine and demand they stand down, but they pay no heed.

The mob is now moving fast towards [yusuf.GetFirstName], and I and my guards have little time to react."

before:
VIETkemet.0003.desc:0 "After changing into humbler clothes, my companions and I now look like ordinary if well-off travelers. The villagers are hospitable to us "travelers" and happily provide us accommodations. It is auspicious that we have come at this time, they say.

Standing in the village square, in the midst of a throng of men, women, and children, I watch as the feast to Osiris proceeds. Some villagers take pigs with them and bring the animals before an altar of the god. They slit the throats of the unfortunate beasts, an offering no doubt to Osiris, before giving the carcasses to swineherds who take the bodies away.

Afterwards, a great cheer erupts, as everyone begins to fill the village square to celebrate. I enjoy drinking good beer and dancing with the other villagers. Soon enough, one villager, playing the flutes, happily skips around playing a lively tune, and we all follow after him while singing praises to Osiris."

before: RICE_bamian_repair_shahr_e_zohak_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Shahr-e Zohak is one of the most impressive fortifications ever built in Afghanistan; one scholar even called it the "Afghan Krak des Chevaliers." It was occupied by successive groups, such as the Hephthalites, Ghaznavids, Ghurids, and Timurids. Zohak is an evil figure in Persian mythology, and though it is uncertain why the fortress is named after him, he is said to be the ancestor of the nearby Ghurids. A legend has it that the fortress city was destroyed by Genghis Khan, and all its inhabitants massacred as revenge for his grandson's death when it was besieged."

before: breton.0028.desc:0 "I am almost finished with the Tro Breizh, for I now arrive in Vannes, the seventh and last stop on this pilgrimage. It is, despite being a very ancient settlement - dating to before the Roman Emperors, learned men tell me - a very joyous and exciting place as well. I found, for example, much amusement in the comically puffy, ugly granite statues the locals dub "Vannes and his Wife." Some of the locals also explained the lore of the ancient large stones that dot the area.\n\nBut this is a time for religion, not mirth. I reflect on the Saint of Vannes, Saint Patern. They say this Saint was a contemporary of the mighty King Arthur, the great Briton hero; he tamed the king's avarice and humbled the monarch according to the legends. At any rate, I too, must practice the virtues. This is why I went on this pilgrimage after all."

before: RICE_bozo_mud_masons_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Mudbricks have been a conspicuous part of buildings in West Africa for centuries, with the Mosque of Djenne as perhaps the most famous example of this style of architecture. Mud masons are respected throughout the region for their practical, spiritual, and sorcerous knowledge, as construction requires not only creating the building, but also the use of spells and incantations to bless the site and exorcise evil spirits. For example, many mud masons in the city of Jenne are of the Bozo ethnicity, and are well-versed in Islamic Quranic verses and what they refer to as #italic bai bibi#!, or "African secrets," the details of which they seldom disclose to outsiders."

before: RICE_bozo_move_jenne_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Jenne-Jeno ("Old Jenne"), the original site of Jenne, was a major urban center in present-day Mali but was abandoned sometime in the medieval period. According to legend, this move happened when the Soninke migrated to the region; they tried to establish a town near the original site settled by the Bozo, but were met with various natural disasters. They were only able to found the city after an oracle told them to sacrifice a virgin girl by burying her alive in the city walls. The tomb of this girl, known as Tapama Djenepo (i.e. "Tapama, the Martyr of Djenne"), still stands in modern Jenne."

before:
bao.0001.desc:0 "My soldiers bring forth two young black-costumed men whom they arrested outside my residence.

"This low-born rabble was found sleeping in a dried ditch, my [ROOT.Char.GetLadyLord]," one of my soldiers says when asked who they are. "They say they are church musicians, but they were acting suspiciously, and it is clear they are highway robbers who are using your property without permission."

Another soldier interjects, "While I do agree they are acting suspiciously, we shouldn't be too hasty to make any judgment.

The first soldier ignores the other's comment, and says, "They are highwaymen, whether you like it or not, so I suggest we give them a swift exemplary punishment for trespassing.""

before: bao.0001.info:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Up until the mid XXth century, costumes were the most reliable way to tell the social status of a stranger; in Brittany, black costumes were un-embroided costumes for the poorest of the poor. The "Sonerien Du" or "Black Musicians" were traveling singers and musicians paid mostly in food and drink, who went from church to church, mass to mass, and wedding to wedding to do their trade. They had the reputation of playing "hep diskrog" or "restlessly" and according to local superstition, a Breton wedding could only end when the musician was too drunk to play. They often were seen as troublemakers by the Gendarmes and the upper stratas of Breton society.\n The actual "Sonerien Du" legend which is the reference for the event is the legend of the Bro Vigouden (Barony of Kemper) where two black-coated musicians were unjustly punished around 1790 in Pont-'n-Abad (Pont-l'-Abbé in French) and sentenced to death for sleeping dead drunk in the roadside, either because they were mistaken for highway robbers or as the result of the corruption of the local aristocracy. Their bodies were exposed on spikes for everyone to see. Because this event coincided with (unverified) plague outbreaks, people held them as martyrs, and would touch the bodies, believing it would grant plague immunity."

before:
socotra.0009.desc:0 "We have tolerated the presence of pirates in my territories for far too long. Our "agreements" with them have not been working in our favor, and even though many are also respectable merchants, can we really trust them when they are no less greedier than the average charlatan and bandit?

I have thus sent out an order to immediately renege on any of our agreements with pirate groups in the [GetGeographicalRegion('RICE_indian_ocean_region').GetName]. before: RICE_galicia_pray_to_santiago_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! before:
normandy.0091.info:0 "
#emphasis Historical Context:#! Whatever the truth of William and Matilda's relationship, there are legends of questionable veracity about how it began. Supposedly, Matilda rejected William's offer of marriage, as she saw herself, daughter of the Count Baldwin of Flanders, as too high-born for a "bastard."

The Duke, in his rage, went all the way to her home in Flanders. In some versions of the legend, he found her going to church and, in broad daylight, dragged her off her horse by her braids and pushed her into the mud before riding off. In other variations, he went to her father's manor, and dragged her by her braids or hit her in full view of everyone, Baldwin included. Afterwards, Matilda bizarrely only wanted to marry William.

In reality, the marriage was probably arranged under more mundane political circumstances. The Counts of Flanders were powerful, and a potential threat to Normandy's east. By marrying into their family, William not only avoided conflict with them, but also gained a valuable ally."

before: RICE_pamir_restore_hephthalite_empire_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! The Hephthalites, sometimes called the White Huns, were a major wave of "Hunnic" tribal invaders into Persia and India in the 4th and 5th centuries. Their relationship with "Hunnic" groups like the Kidarites and Xionites, the ethnic differences between these groups (if any), and where they came from, is still debated in academic circles - there are too many theories to be listed here, but suffice to say, Iranian and Turkic influence in their origins is likely, and it is possible that the Pamirs are their homeland. A Persian and Turkic alliance defeated them in c. 560 CE and the Hephthalite Empire split into many petty chiefdoms. Prominent among these Hephthalite rump states were the Turkshahis and their cousins, the Zunbils."

before:
harran.0062.desc:0 "I sit in the darkness of my library, sipping mint tea as my acquaintance enters the room. He is a scholar from the House of Wisdom who I worked with back when I lived in Baghdad, and he gives a smile as he joins me. I offer him some tea, and we chat pleasantly about various topics to catch up.

Eventually, our conversation drifts towards the topic of religion. "I heard something interesting about your grandfather [hilal_al_sabi.GetFullName] the other day," my friend tells me.

This again? I shift uncomfortably, but don't say anything yet, and continue sipping my tea."

before:
harran.0063.desc:0 "“You have said for many years that your grandfather converted to Islam thanks to a dream, a sure sign from Allah himself.” My friend smiles. "One of my mentors, an older gentleman, who was acquainted with your grandfather, said he never heard of such a thing, but admits perhaps his memory is not as it used to be thanks to old age. I don’t doubt you, but it does make me wonder if your grandfather was telling the truth - no offense to him.” 

I stroke my chin and gaze at my friend quietly. Many question my grandfather's story. I know this.

I ponder how to respond."

before:
harran.0065.desc:0 "“But what?” he says.

I frown.

"I don't mean to imply he was secretly an apostate, but…." I consider my words carefully. "I always felt he had sympathy for his birth religion. I could tell by the way he talked fondly of our ancestors."

"The scholarly achievements of Harran's pagans are nothing to laugh at! Your forebear, [thabit_ibn_qurra.GetFullName], was a rare scholar of his age." My friend nods. "But if your grandfather's heart is genuine, thanks to that dream, then that is all that matters. Sure, you still have a few wayward relatives who still believe your old gods, and I know you were never the most pious man, but at least you are a believer, too, right?""

before: RICE_yazd_city_of_windcatchers_desc:0 "Due to Yazd‘s location along the edge of the #italic Dasht-e Kavir#! desert, windcatchers - tall towers that trap and channel air to provide natural ventilation and cooling - are ubiquitous in the city, giving rise to its nickname, "City of Windcatchers." before: RICE_khuzestan_khuzi_status_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Early medieval Islamic sources mention the existence of a so-called Khuzi people, who spoke a language that modern scholars theorize to be a late remnant of ancient Elamite. Although Khuzi was spoken by local nobility, this may have been because they learned it from their servants (such as wet-nurses, bathroom attendants, and so on). The Khuzis were otherwise treated as low status; for example, #italic "yā Xuz̄ı!"#!, meaning "Hey, you Khuzi!" was reported by the 10th century Arab geographer Al-Maqdisi as a common, slang term of insult in the region. Because of this, the Khuzi identity and language likely faded away as the Khuzis assimilated into Arab or Iranian populations."
after: RICE_khuzestan_khuzi_status_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Early medieval Islamic sources mention the existence of a so-called Khuzi people, who spoke a language that modern scholars theorize to be a late remnant of ancient Elamite. Although Khuzi was spoken by local nobility, this may have been because they learned it from their servants (such as wet-nurses, bathroom attendants, and so on). The Khuzis were otherwise treated as low status; for example, #italic \"yā Xuz̄ı!\"#!, meaning \"Hey, you Khuzi!\" was reported by the 10th century Arab geographer Al-Maqdisi as a common, slang term of insult in the region. Because of this, the Khuzi identity and language likely faded away as the Khuzis assimilated into Arab or Iranian populations."

before:
north_atlantic.0208.info:0 "
#emphasis Historical Context:#! Dairy products have been consumed in Northern and Western Europe for centuries, and #italic skyr#! is the name of the Icelandic variant of yogurt. Interestingly, in the Icelandic sagas, serving items like milk, cheese, or yogurt to guests was considered improper, particularly if other food could be provided. Being immersed in milk products could be considered especially humiliating.

In one episode of the #italic Egil's Saga#!, for instance, the protagonist Egil and his companions visit a man named Armod, who only serves them #italic skyr#!. Egil takes this as a great insult, and, in revenge, vomits the yogurt all over Armod, who in turn vomits back at Egil. When Armod's men ask why Egil did such a thing, he says, "Don’t blame me for following the master of the house’s example. He’s spewing his guts out just as much as I am.""

before:
north_atlantic.0273.desc:0 "Though I am young, I have already learned much from the schools here in the British Isles. I have greater ambitions, however, when it comes to scholarly matters; my knowledge of mathematics, various languages, and especially astronomy will carry me far, as I seek to better understand the great universe which [ROOT.Char.GetFaith.HighGodName] created.

The skies are marked with numberless sparks, each a fire, and I know these stars well. I have seen in these stars that it is perhaps my time to travel far from here, and learn more and more about this world. Maybe, one day, I can even become one of the greatest astrologers in the world.

#weak "Every astrologer is worthy of praise and honor, since by such a doctrine as astrology, he knows many secrets of [ROOT.Char.GetFaith.HighGodName], and things which few know."#!"

before:
normandy.0091.info:0 "
#emphasis Historical Context:#! Whatever the truth of William and Matilda's relationship, there are legends of questionable veracity about how it began. Supposedly, Matilda rejected William's offer of marriage, as she saw herself, daughter of the Count Baldwin of Flanders, as too high-born for a "bastard."

The Duke, in his rage, went all the way to her home in Flanders. In some versions of the legend, he found her going to church and, in broad daylight, dragged her off her horse by her braids and pushed her into the mud before riding off. In other variations, he went to her father's manor, and dragged her by her braids or hit her in full view of everyone, Baldwin included. Afterwards, Matilda bizarrely only wanted to marry William.

In reality, the marriage was probably arranged under more mundane political circumstances. The Counts of Flanders were powerful, and a potential threat to Normandy's east. By marrying into their family, William not only avoided conflict with them, but also gained a valuable ally."

before: RICE_sri_lanka_worship_local_deities_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! For centuries, the people of Sri Lanka have worshipped a variety of shared deities, regardless of whether they are Buddhist or Hindu, or Sinhala, Tamil, or Vedda. Many of these deities were syncretized forms of Hindu, Buddhist, and indigenous religious figures, known by different names from different communities and often worshipped in a manner distinct from mainland India. I have thus sent out an order to immediately renege on any of our agreements with pirate groups in the [GetGeographicalRegion('RICE_indian_ocean_region').GetName]. before: RICE_bamian_repair_shahr_e_zohak_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Shahr-e Zohak is one of the most impressive fortifications ever built in Afghanistan; one scholar even called it the "Afghan Krak des Chevaliers." It was occupied by successive groups, such as the Hephthalites, Ghaznavids, Ghurids, and Timurids. Zohak is an evil figure in Persian mythology, and though it is uncertain why the fortress is named after him, he is said to be the ancestor of the nearby Ghurids. "This low-born rabble was found sleeping in a dried ditch, my [ROOT.Char.GetLadyLord]," one of my soldiers says when asked who they are. "They say they are church musicians, but they were acting suspiciously, and it is clear they are highway robbers who are using your property without permission."

before: bao.0001.info:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Up until the mid XXth century, costumes were the most reliable way to tell the social status of a stranger; in Brittany, black costumes were un-embroided costumes for the poorest of the poor. The "Sonerien Du" or "Black Musicians" were traveling singers and musicians paid mostly in food and drink, who went from church to church, mass to mass, and wedding to wedding to do their trade. They had the reputation of playing "hep diskrog" or "restlessly" and according to local superstition, a Breton wedding could only end when the musician was too drunk to play. They often were seen as troublemakers by the Gendarmes and the upper stratas of Breton society.\n The actual "Sonerien Du" legend which is the reference for the event is the legend of the Bro Vigouden (Barony of Kemper) where two black-coated musicians were unjustly punished around 1790 in Pont-'n-Abad (Pont-l'-Abbé in French) and sentenced to death for sleeping dead drunk in the roadside, either because they were mistaken for highway robbers or as the result of the corruption of the local aristocracy. Their bodies were exposed on spikes for everyone to see. Because this event coincided with (unverified) plague outbreaks, people held them as martyrs, and would touch the bodies, believing it would grant plague immunity."

before: breton.0028.desc:0 "I am almost finished with the Tro Breizh, for I now arrive in Vannes, the seventh and last stop on this pilgrimage. It is, despite being a very ancient settlement - dating to before the Roman Emperors, learned men tell me - a very joyous and exciting place as well. I found, for example, much amusement in the comically puffy, ugly granite statues the locals dub "Vannes and his Wife." Some of the locals also explained the lore of the ancient large stones that dot the area.\n\nBut this is a time for religion, not mirth. I reflect on the Saint of Vannes, Saint Patern. They say this Saint was a contemporary of the mighty King Arthur, the great Briton hero; he tamed the king's avarice and humbled the monarch according to the legends. At any rate, I too, must practice the virtues. This is why I went on this pilgrimage after all."

before: RICE_granada_alhambra_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! The Alhambra (from Arabic #italic Al-Hamra#!, meaning "the Red One") was a palace and fortress complex of the Nasrid dynasty of Granada, and the epitome of medieval Moorish architecture. As a self-contained city, it had its own amenities likes bathhouses and mosques, and was continually expanded by the Nasrids from the 13th to 15th centuries. A striking element of the Alhambra is how many of its walls, columns, fountains, and other surfaces are covered in Quranic verses or poetry from poets of the time, writen in Arabic calligraphy."

before:
granada.0014.desc:0 "I was sleeping at my manor in [granada.GetNameNoTier] when my guards woke me late at night - chaos has erupted in the city's streets!

Apparently, a false rumor had spread earlier today that the Jewish official [yusuf.GetFullName] and other Jews had defected to an enemy ruler, opened the city gates, and killed me. Thanks to recent, rising anti-Jewish sentiment, a mob quickly formed to "protect" the city. Obviously, I’m alive and [granada.GetNameNoTierNoTooltip] is safe.

Before I know it, [yusuf.GetFirstName] arrives in a panic, begging for help. Moments later, the mob storms my palace, screaming how they will kill the "traitor" [yusuf.GetFirstName] before going for his fellow Jews next. I rush to meet the mob to reassure them that I am fine and demand they stand down, but they pay no heed.

The mob is now moving fast towards [yusuf.GetFirstName], and I and my guards have little time to react."

before:
khwarezm.0014.desc:0 "The citadel of Al-Fir in [kath.GetNameNoTier] has stood proudly for many years. This beautiful and mighty fortress can be seen for miles and miles, and served as a symbol of the local rulers' might and prestige. Alas, it also happens to be located next to the Amu Darya or Oxus River, nicknamed the "Mad River" due to its tendency to change course or overflood erratically.

Over the years, the citadel has managed to withstand assault after assault by the waters of the Oxus, but its defenses have gradually worn out. Though the main structure of the fortress is still standing, it is partly ruined, and local authorities have deemed it no longer safe to use on a large scale, and the administration has relocated to other structures in town.

Still, at least the citadel remains standing. Even if it is no longer in frequent use, it will surely continue to inspire and embolden the inhabitants nearby."

before: RICE_pamir_restore_hephthalite_empire_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! The Hephthalites, sometimes called the White Huns, were a major wave of "Hunnic" tribal invaders into Persia and India in the 4th and 5th centuries. Their relationship with "Hunnic" groups like the Kidarites and Xionites, the ethnic differences between these groups (if any), and where they came from, is still debated in academic circles - there are too many theories to be listed here, but suffice to say, Iranian and Turkic influence in their origins is likely, and it is possible that the Pamirs are their homeland. A Persian and Turkic alliance defeated them in c. 560 CE and the Hephthalite Empire split into many petty chiefdoms. Prominent among these Hephthalite rump states were the Turkshahis and their cousins, the Zunbils."

before:
north_atlantic.0208.info:0 "
#emphasis Historical Context:#! Dairy products have been consumed in Northern and Western Europe for centuries, and #italic skyr#! is the name of the Icelandic variant of yogurt. Interestingly, in the Icelandic sagas, serving items like milk, cheese, or yogurt to guests was considered improper, particularly if other food could be provided. Being immersed in milk products could be considered especially humiliating.

In one episode of the #italic Egil's Saga#!, for instance, the protagonist Egil and his companions visit a man named Armod, who only serves them #italic skyr#!. Egil takes this as a great insult, and, in revenge, vomits the yogurt all over Armod, who in turn vomits back at Egil. When Armod's men ask why Egil did such a thing, he says, "Don’t blame me for following the master of the house’s example. He’s spewing his guts out just as much as I am.""

before:
north_atlantic.0273.desc:0 "Though I am young, I have already learned much from the schools here in the British Isles. I have greater ambitions, however, when it comes to scholarly matters; my knowledge of mathematics, various languages, and especially astronomy will carry me far, as I seek to better understand the great universe which [ROOT.Char.GetFaith.HighGodName] created.

The skies are marked with numberless sparks, each a fire, and I know these stars well. I have seen in these stars that it is perhaps my time to travel far from here, and learn more and more about this world. Maybe, one day, I can even become one of the greatest astrologers in the world.

#weak "Every astrologer is worthy of praise and honor, since by such a doctrine as astrology, he knows many secrets of [ROOT.Char.GetFaith.HighGodName], and things which few know."#!"

before: RICE_khuzestan_khuzi_status_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Early medieval Islamic sources mention the existence of a so-called Khuzi people, who spoke a language that modern scholars theorize to be a late remnant of ancient Elamite. Although Khuzi was spoken by local nobility, this may have been because they learned it from their servants (such as wet-nurses, bathroom attendants, and so on). The Khuzis were otherwise treated as low status; for example, #italic "yā Xuz̄ı!"#!, meaning "Hey, you Khuzi!" was reported by the 10th century Arab geographer Al-Maqdisi as a common, slang term of insult in the region. Because of this, the Khuzi identity and language likely faded away as the Khuzis assimilated into Arab or Iranian populations."
after: RICE_khuzestan_khuzi_status_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Early medieval Islamic sources mention the existence of a so-called Khuzi people, who spoke a language that modern scholars theorize to be a late remnant of ancient Elamite. Although Khuzi was spoken by local nobility, this may have been because they learned it from their servants (such as wet-nurses, bathroom attendants, and so on). The Khuzis were otherwise treated as low status; for example, #italic \"yā Xuz̄ı!\"#!, meaning \"Hey, you Khuzi!\" was reported by the 10th century Arab geographer Al-Maqdisi as a common, slang term of insult in the region. Because of this, the Khuzi identity and language likely faded away as the Khuzis assimilated into Arab or Iranian populations."

before: RICE_bozo_mud_masons_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Mudbricks have been a conspicuous part of buildings in West Africa for centuries, with the Mosque of Djenne as perhaps the most famous example of this style of architecture. Mud masons are respected throughout the region for their practical, spiritual, and sorcerous knowledge, as construction requires not only creating the building, but also the use of spells and incantations to bless the site and exorcise evil spirits. For example, many mud masons in the city of Jenne are of the Bozo ethnicity, and are well-versed in Islamic Quranic verses and what they refer to as #italic bai bibi#!, or "African secrets," the details of which they seldom disclose to outsiders."

before: RICE_bozo_move_jenne_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Jenne-Jeno ("Old Jenne"), the original site of Jenne, was a major urban center in present-day Mali but was abandoned sometime in the medieval period. According to legend, this move happened when the Soninke migrated to the region; they tried to establish a town near the original site settled by the Bozo, but were met with various natural disasters. They were only able to found the city after an oracle told them to sacrifice a virgin girl by burying her alive in the city walls. The tomb of this girl, known as Tapama Djenepo (i.e. "Tapama, the Martyr of Djenne"), still stands in modern Jenne."

before: RICE_yazd_city_of_windcatchers_desc:0 "Due to Yazd‘s location along the edge of the #italic Dasht-e Kavir#! desert, windcatchers - tall towers that trap and channel air to provide natural ventilation and cooling - are ubiquitous in the city, giving rise to its nickname, "City of Windcatchers." The city is also known for its large network of qanat waterways, and its qanat makers are said to be some of the most skilled across Iran. Overall, Yazd‘s infrastructure - including its windcatchers, qanats, ab anbar cisterns, yakhchal ice houses, and more - make it not only livable, but also comfortable.\n\nThe costs of building a qanat for the [ruler|E] of Yazd is reduced when taking the [decision|E] to #V Fund the Construction of a Qanat#!"

before: rice_vajrayana_canon_doctrine_desc:0 "The Tantric Canon is the collection of Buddhist texts accepted by the so-called esoteric schools of Buddhism, such as Tibetan Vajrayana and sects influenced by them. The Tibetan Canon for example consists of the Kangyur ("Translation of the Word") and Tengyur ("Translation of Treatises"). These canons include Mahayana texts, as well as texts from early schools of Buddhism that are not part of or were discarded from the Pali Canon."

before:
harran.0062.desc:0 "I sit in the darkness of my library, sipping mint tea as my acquaintance enters the room. He is a scholar from the House of Wisdom who I worked with back when I lived in Baghdad, and he gives a smile as he joins me. I offer him some tea, and we chat pleasantly about various topics to catch up.

Eventually, our conversation drifts towards the topic of religion. "I heard something interesting about your grandfather [hilal_al_sabi.GetFullName] the other day," my friend tells me.

This again? I shift uncomfortably, but don't say anything yet, and continue sipping my tea."

before:
harran.0063.desc:0 "“You have said for many years that your grandfather converted to Islam thanks to a dream, a sure sign from Allah himself.” My friend smiles. "One of my mentors, an older gentleman, who was acquainted with your grandfather, said he never heard of such a thing, but admits perhaps his memory is not as it used to be thanks to old age. I don’t doubt you, but it does make me wonder if your grandfather was telling the truth - no offense to him.” 

I stroke my chin and gaze at my friend quietly. Many question my grandfather's story. I know this.

I ponder how to respond."

before:
harran.0065.desc:0 "“But what?” he says.

I frown.

"I don't mean to imply he was secretly an apostate, but…." I consider my words carefully. "I always felt he had sympathy for his birth religion. I could tell by the way he talked fondly of our ancestors."

"The scholarly achievements of Harran's pagans are nothing to laugh at! Your forebear, [thabit_ibn_qurra.GetFullName], was a rare scholar of his age." My friend nods. "But if your grandfather's heart is genuine, thanks to that dream, then that is all that matters. Sure, you still have a few wayward relatives who still believe your old gods, and I know you were never the most pious man, but at least you are a believer, too, right?""

before:
VIETkemet.0003.desc:0 "After changing into humbler clothes, my companions and I now look like ordinary if well-off travelers. The villagers are hospitable to us "travelers" and happily provide us accommodations. It is auspicious that we have come at this time, they say.

Standing in the village square, in the midst of a throng of men, women, and children, I watch as the feast to Osiris proceeds. Some villagers take pigs with them and bring the animals before an altar of the god. They slit the throats of the unfortunate beasts, an offering no doubt to Osiris, before giving the carcasses to swineherds who take the bodies away.

Afterwards, a great cheer erupts, as everyone begins to fill the village square to celebrate. I enjoy drinking good beer and dancing with the other villagers. Soon enough, one villager, playing the flutes, happily skips around playing a lively tune, and we all follow after him while singing praises to Osiris."

before:
VIETkemet.0011.desc:0 "The sorcerer-priest understands my worries, and knows the right incantation for my situation. He thus begins to chant in my presence:

"I am bringing the gods incense and natron.
I want to expel the bad smell from your mouth.
Therefore I come in order to expel the evil in your hearts.
With this I remove the Evil, Isfet, which clings to you.
With this I bring you Good.
I present Justice, Maat, to you......""

before: RICE_red_sea_chew_khat_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Khat (or qat) is a leaf which is chewed as a stimulant in parts of East Africa and Yemen where the plant is native. before: game_concept_sicily_three_worlds_desc:1 "Historically, the medieval [RICE_sicily_struggle|E] was influenced in various ways by the "three worlds" – the [sicily_latin|E], [sicily_greek|E], and [sicily_arabic|E] worlds. In-game, they are represented by the colors blue, purple, and green respectively.\n\nThe three worlds' influence is reflected by each world's #bold Dominance#!, an abstracted, global value. [rulers|E] cannot directly change Dominance values. The values merely reflect how many [rulers|E], [counties|E], or [sicily_strongholds_short|E] in [RICE_sicily_struggle_short|E] are of each world, as well as the [trait_level_track_xp|E] of [rulers|E] in the [GetTrait('RICE_sicilian_ruler').GetName( GetNullCharacter )] [trait|E]."

before: RICE_sicily_second_pavia_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Pavia was the capital of the Lombard Kingdom that dominated Italy from the 6th to 8th centuries, until its defeat by the Carolingian Franks. Lombard successor states emerged in southern Italy, and Benevento, a major center of Lombard power there, was even known as a "second Pavia" due to its prosperity and prominence. Ironically, these same Lombard polities were often dominated by the Franks to the north. The Lombards in the south would remain a distinct identity up until the era of Norman Sicily in the 12th and 13th centuries."
after: RICE_sicily_second_pavia_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! The Lombards in the south would remain a distinct identity up until the era of Norman Sicily in the 12th and 13th centuries."

before: RICE_sicily_byzantine_syracuse_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! Syracuse was one of the great cities of the ancient Mediterranean; Cicero, for instance, described it as "the greatest Greek city and the most beautiful of them all." It retained its importance during the early Byzantine period, particularly after the empire's loss of its African territories; it even briefly served as the capital of the empire from 663-669 CE. With the Muslim conquest of Sicily, including the fall of Syracuse in 878, the island's center moved to Palermo, and while Syracuse still remained a major city on the island, it never regained its former preeminent status."
after: RICE_sicily_byzantine_syracuse_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! With the Muslim conquest of Sicily, including the fall of Syracuse in 878, the island's center moved to Palermo, and while Syracuse still remained a major city on the island, it never regained its former preeminent status."

before: RICE_sicily_catania_elephant_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Historical Context:#! #italic U Liotru#! is a famous elephant statue in the city of Catania. The name is a corruption of Heliodorus, a legendary 8th century necromancer and sorcerer who either brought the statue to life, or transformed into it himself, before he was defeated by Saint Leo of Catania. Though the legend is of dubious historicity, the city has been associated with the statue for centuries; the Arabs called Catania the "city of the Elephant," and the geographer al-Idrisi, who worked at the court of King Roger II of Sicily, believed the statue was made by the Carthaginians or Romans and that the Catanese considered the statue to be magical and able to protect them from Mount Etna's eruptions. In 1239, the statue was chosen to be the city's symbol. After an earthquake, it was repurposed into a fountain in 1737."

before: sicily.0001.desc:0 ""Sicily was the first of our provinces; Sicily first taught our ancestors how glorious it could be to rule other peoples." So said the great Roman Cicero, long before Rome declined in the West.\n\nSicily, crucible of the Mediterranean, is now a wild frontier where three worlds meet: Islam, Byzantium, and the Latin West. Many covet Sicily and its abundance, but would-be conquerors and settlers often find behind this paradise is a liminal land where the boundaries between culture, faith, and loyalty can be very blurry."

before:
yorkshire.0106.desc:0 "I am reflecting over the life and times of Alcuin, that famous scholar and monk from York and who became an important intellectual of Charlemagne’s court. He trained many important thinkers of his era, and I feel a little sense of pride at the thought that I rule territories not too far from where he was born and grew up in. Two of his famous sayings, I recall, include:

"Remember to care for the soul more than the body, since the former remains, the latter perishes."

"And do not listen to those who keep saying, 'The voice of the people is the voice of God', because the tumult of the crowd is always close to madness.""

before:
lesbos.0051.desc:0 "We have tolerated the presence of pirates in my territories for far too long. Our "agreements" with them have not been working in our favor, and even though many are also respectable merchants, can we really trust them when they are no less greedier than the average charlatan and bandit?

I have thus sent out an order to immediately renege on any of our agreements with pirate groups in the [GetGeographicalRegion('RICE_mediterranean_region').GetName]. They will no longer be afforded legal protections nor the ability to set up their base of operations in my territories by working with us, because they no longer work #italic for#! us.

I have ordered my troops to make sure these pirates comply with our commands. We can only hope they leave peaceably...."

before:
khwarezm.0014.desc:0 "The citadel of Al-Fir in [kath.GetNameNoTier] has stood proudly for many years. This beautiful and mighty fortress can be seen for miles and miles, and served as a symbol of the local rulers' might and prestige. Alas, it also happens to be located next to the Amu Darya or Oxus River, nicknamed the "Mad River" due to its tendency to change course or overflood erratically.

Over the years, the citadel has managed to withstand assault after assault by the waters of the Oxus, but its defenses have gradually worn out. Though the main structure of the fortress is still standing, it is partly ruined, and local authorities have deemed it no longer safe to use on a large scale, and the administration has relocated to other structures in town.

Still, at least the citadel remains standing. Even if it is no longer in frequent use, it will surely continue to inspire and embolden the inhabitants nearby."

before: sardinia.0060.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte Historique :#! Dans l'Antiquité et au Moyen Âge, la Sardaigne avait une mauvaise réputation en raison de l'épidémie de paludisme qui sévissait sur l'île et du stéréotype selon lequel ses habitants (quelle que soit leur origine) étaient plutôt féroces et têtus, voire avaient des tendances criminelles.\n\nAinsi, lorsque l'archevêque pisan Frédéric Visconti, qui détenait l'autorité ecclésiastique sur l'île, s'apprête à la visiter en 1263, il déclare : "Comment allons-nous nous débrouiller dans cette terre d'horreur et de solitude, où les gens ne vont que pour faire un bon profit ?" et que "la Sardaigne était malade, et même la maladie personnifiée, car tous ceux qui quittent l'endroit tombent rapidement malades"."

Djenné-Djeno ("Vieux Djenné"), le site d'origine de Djenné, était un centre urbain important dans l'actuel Mali, mais il a été abandonné au cours de la période médiévale. Selon la légende, ce déplacement s'est produit lorsque les Soninkés ont migré dans la région ; ils ont tenté d'établir une ville près du site d'origine colonisé par les Bozo, mais ont dû faire face à diverses catastrophes naturelles. Ils n'ont pu fonder la ville qu'après qu'un oracle leur a dit de sacrifier une jeune fille vierge en l'enterrant vivante dans les murs de la ville. La tombe de cette jeune fille, connue sous le nom de Tapama Djenepo (c'est-à-dire "Tapama, la martyre de Djenné"), se trouve toujours dans la ville moderne de Djenné."

before: red_sea.0037.desc:0 "Je reçois un grand aristocrate musulman qui vient d'achever son pèlerinage à la Mecque et qui rentre maintenant chez lui. Alors que je lui demande de me raconter son aventure, il me dit que la partie la plus effrayante du voyage a été la traversée de la mer Rouge en ferry.\n\n"Je n'avais jamais été en mer auparavant ", explique-t-il. "J'ai dû m'accrocher à mon esclave pour ne pas vomir pendant tout ce temps. Elle est née dans un pays côtier, vous voyez, et habituée à être sur un bateau, et elle s'est moquée de moi pour ma faiblesse - j'aurais pu fouetter la fille fougueuse à ce moment-là si je n'avais pas eu de l'affection pour elle... ou peut-être que j'étais juste trop nauséeux pour répondre....""

before: RICE_sicily_byzantine_syracuse_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! Syracuse était l'une des grandes villes de la Méditerranée antique ; Cicéron, par exemple, la décrivait comme "la plus grande ville grecque et la plus belle de toutes". Elle a conservé son importance au début de la période byzantine, en particulier après la perte par l'empire de ses territoires africains ; elle a même brièvement servi de capitale à l'empire de 663 à 669. Avec la conquête musulmane de la Sicile, et notamment la chute de Syracuse en 878, le centre de l'île s'est déplacé à Palerme, et si Syracuse est restée une ville importante de l'île, elle n'a jamais retrouvé son statut prééminent d'antan."

before: RICE_sicily_catania_elephant_decision_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! #italic U Liotru#! est une célèbre statue d'éléphant dans la ville de Catane. Le nom est une corruption d'Héliodore, un nécromancien et sorcier légendaire du VIIIe siècle qui a donné vie à la statue ou s'est transformé en elle avant d'être vaincu par Saint Léon de Catane. Bien que la légende soit d'une historicité douteuse, la ville est associée à la statue depuis des siècles ; les Arabes appelaient Catane la "ville de l'éléphant", et le géographe al-Idrisi, qui travaillait à la cour du roi Roger II de Sicile, pensait que la statue avait été fabriquée par les Carthaginois ou les Romains et que les Catanais la considéraient comme magique et capable de les protéger contre les éruptions de l'Etna. En 1239, la statue a été choisie comme symbole de la ville. Après un tremblement de terre, elle a été transformée en fontaine en 1737."

before: sicily.0001.desc:0 "La Sicile a été la première de nos provinces ; la Sicile a enseigné à nos ancêtres combien il pouvait être glorieux de gouverner d'autres peuples". Ainsi s'exprimait le grand Romain Cicéron, bien avant le déclin de Rome en Occident.\n\nLa Sicile, creuset de la Méditerranée, est aujourd'hui une frontière sauvage où trois mondes se rencontrent : L'Islam, Byzance et l'Occident latin. before:
sicily.0181.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! #italic Ayo visto lo mappamundi#! ou #italic Aggiu vistu lu mappamundu#!, qui se traduit par "J'ai vu la carte du monde", est une chanson folklorique sicilienne populaire à la cour d'Alphonse V d'Aragon, à l'époque où l'Aragon régnait sur une grande partie de l'Italie méridionale.

La chanson est une parodie d'une lauda moralisatrice (un genre de chant religieux vernaculaire en italien médiéval et de la Renaissance) du poète florentin Feo Belcari (1410 - 1484), chantée sur le même air. Les paroles de la chanson, qui mentionnent d'autres belles terres qui n'impressionnent pas le narrateur autant que la Sicile, comportent également un jeu de mots basé sur un jeu de mots entre Cicilia (orthographe historique de Sicile) et Cecilia, qui fait référence à la fois à Sainte Cécile et à l'amante du narrateur.

Le compositeur espagnol Juan Cornago (vers 1400 - vers 1475) a composé une messe sur l'air de la chanson, qui est notre seule source de la mélodie originale de la chanson. La chanson originale a été reconstituée plus récemment par des érudits."

before: sicily.0200.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! Dans le monde médiéval, les régions multiculturelles avaient souvent des courts différentes au service des diverses communautés ethniques et religieuses, en raison des différences de traditions juridiques. Dans la Sicile du haut Moyen Âge, les habitants avaient tendance à s'adresser au tribunal qu'ils jugeaient le plus avantageux pour eux, indépendamment de leur "appartenance" à ce groupe. En d'autres termes, un Arabe musulman pouvait s'adresser à une court greque chrétienne pour résoudre un litige, ou vice versa.\n\nLa fréquence de ces cas suggère plusieurs choses. Premièrement, les identités des personnes étaient intentionnellement malléables et vacillantes, ne serait-ce qu'au sens juridique du terme. Deuxièmement, les gens étaient conscients des différences entre les différents groupes religieux et ethniques. Troisièmement, les courts de ces différents groupes avaient suffisamment d'autorité pour appliquer les lois conformément à leurs propres traditions."

before:
sicily.0201.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! Dans l'islam médiéval, la Sicile était considérée comme une zone frontalière entre le #italic Dar al-Islam#!, la maison de l'islam, et le #italic Dar al-Harb#!, la maison de la guerre, où vivaient les non-croyants. Parfois, le terme #italic thagr al-jihad#!, c'est-à-dire le "port de la guerre sainte", était utilisé pour décrire cette région.

Par exemple, Ibn Hamis, un poète arabe sicilien (1056 - 1133), a utilisé ce terme dans ses poèmes. Ayant fui la Sicile dans sa jeunesse à la suite des invasions normandes, ses poèmes évoquent souvent la nostalgie de sa patrie paradisiaque.

Toutefois, si l'on met de côté les aspects théologiques et idéologiques de ces termes, dans la pratique, le monde islamique a réagi de diverses manières quant à la façon de se comporter et de vivre dans de telles contrées."

before:
sicily.0202.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! Certaines sources chrétiennes #italic et#! musulmanes médiévales décrivent leurs coreligionnaires siciliens en termes désobligeants, en raison de leur tolérance religieuse ou de leur manque de conviction et de connaissance spirituelles.

Par exemple, l'érudit et voyageur musulman du Xe siècle, Ibn Hawqal, décrit les Siciliens musulmans en des termes très peu flatteurs : ils sont, selon lui, stupides, cupides et trop désireux de se mélanger et de se marier avec des chrétiens. Il se moque également des érudits musulmans siciliens qui auraient oublié les principes de base de l'islam.

Plus tard, au XIIIe siècle, l'empereur Frédéric II du Saint-Empire romain germanique, qui a grandi en Sicile et y a établi sa base de pouvoir, a été qualifié de "sultan baptisé". Certains chrétiens #italic et#! musulmans pensaient qu'il était un musulman secret en raison de ses liens avec le monde islamique et de sa connaissance de l'arabe et de l'islam.

Dans une région frontalière sauvage comme la Sicile, un certain degré de tolérance ou au moins une volonté de s'engager dans d'autres "mondes" était nécessaire à la survie. Cependant, les étrangers, qui ne comprenaient pas cette situation complexe, considéraient souvent ce pragmatisme avec suspicion, voire comme des signes de défaillance morale et d'apostasie."

L'Italie méridionale médiévale était une frontière dynamique, en constante évolution, et les dirigeants locaux devaient trouver des moyens d'attirer de nouveaux colons afin d'agrandir et de développer leurs territoires. Par exemple, en 1035 de notre ère, l'émirat kalbide de Sicile a proposé une exonération de l'impôt foncier pour "les gens d'Ifriqiya" - c'est-à-dire ceux qui étaient récemment arrivés d'Afrique du Nord - qui ne s'appliquerait pas aux "gens de Sicile", c'est-à-dire ceux qui vivaient en Sicile depuis un certain temps."

before: sicily.0209.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! Dans la région diversifiée qu'était la Sicile médiévale, les souverains trouvaient souvent plus facile de conserver les lois traditionnelles de leurs sujets, même s'ils étaient d'origines différentes. Par exemple, lorsque le premier roi de Sicile, Roger II (1095 - 1154), a centralisé son pouvoir dans les années 1140 en publiant un code juridique communément mais incorrectement appelé les Assises d'Ariano, il a proclamé dans l'introduction des Assises que "nous ordonnons que les lois nouvellement promulguées... soient pleinement observées par tous. En raison de la diversité des peuples soumis à notre autorité, les usages, les coutumes et les lois qui ont existé parmi eux jusqu'à présent ne sont pas abrogés, à moins que ce qui y est observé ne soit clairement en contradiction avec nos édits ici.""

before:
sicily.0211.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! Bien que Baia ait été un lieu de villégiature populaire dans l'Antiquité et au Moyen Âge, et que ses prétendus bienfaits médicinaux aient été célébrés, même dans les sources religieuses, elle a également été une source de controverse.

Un certain nombre de sources antiques et médiévales condamnaient Baia comme un lieu d'immoralité. Par exemple, l'homme d'État et juriste romain Cicéron, en tant qu'avocat, a un jour miné le témoignage contradictoire d'une femme noble aux mœurs légères en liant ses mœurs légères à Baia.

Même des sources moins critiques ont fait référence à cette réputation. Par exemple, l'écrivain italien du XIVe siècle Giovanni Boccaccio (surtout connu pour son célèbre Décaméron) a utilisé Baia comme décor dans l'un de ses romans, #italic L'élégie de Dame Fiammetta#!. La protagoniste se rend à Baia pour se détendre et oublier son histoire d'amour adultère, mais elle se rend compte que c'est contre-productif car "même les femmes les plus chastes oublient leur pudeur féminine et semblent prendre plus de libertés en toute occasion" à Baia.

Quoi qu'il en soit, les médiévaux étaient très conscients de la réputation de Baia, bonne ou mauvaise, auprès des anciens, et certaines sources médiévales concernant Baia font référence à des sources antiques comme celle de Virgile."

before: sicily.0214.info:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! La Malte médiévale était un important fournisseur de dents de requin fossilisées, connues à l'époque sous le nom de "pierres de langue" ou "langues de serpent". Au cours de la période médiévale, les pierres de langue étaient, entre autres usages médicaux, un remède courant ou une protection contre le poison. À l'époque, la tradition voulait que l'on suspende des pierres de langue à des arbres décoratifs sur les tables pendant les fêtes ; les invités pouvaient tremper les pierres de langue dans leur vin ou leur boisson, assurés qu'ils ne seraient pas empoisonnés."

before: RICE_sus_divert_and_dam_ziz_river_context_tooltip:0 "#emphasis Contexte historique :#! Les preuves géographiques, historiques et archéologiques attestent de l'existence, dans la région de Sijilmassa, d'un vaste système hydraulique composé de canaux, de barrages, de réservoirs, etc... L'expansion continue de ce système, particulièrement durant et après la période Almoravide, permis d'accroitre considérablement les ressources en eau des habitants de Sijilmassa. D'après le folklore local, la clé de voute de ce système était la source Timedrine, dont la destruction par un gouverneur tyrannique surnommé le "Sultan Noir" entraîna le déclin de la cité."

before: sus.0060.desc:0 "Un voyageur de passage m'a raconté comment, dans son pays d'origine, les gens parlent en termes élogieux des pièces produites par les hôtels des monnaies de [sijilmasa_county.GetNameNoTier].\n\n"En vérité", dit-il, "les pièces frappées ici sont de la plus haute qualité. before: sus.0063.desc:0 "Aujourd'hui, je visite certaines des forêts d'arganiers de mon royaume. L'une des femmes locales m'explique que les chèvres, qui grimpent aux arbres pour manger les fruits et les noix, sont très utiles pour extraire les précieuses graines de l'arganier, qui sont utilisées pour fabriquer des huiles, des aliments et bien d'autres choses encore. Traditionnellement, ce sont des femmes comme elle qui travaillent habituellement avec ces arganiers.\n\n"Certains pensent que ce sont les excréments de chèvre qui sont la clé de tout cela" la femme rit, "mais c'est en fait la motte qui nous aide à casser les noix d'argan. before:
lesbos.0029.desc:0 "La voix des enfants chantant des cantiques dehors est impossible à confondre. "Kalendes ! Kalendes !" chantent-ils, comme une mélopée envoûtante.

Chaque fois que de tels enfants se présentent, il est important que nous leur donnions quelques sucreries ou un peu d'or, car telle est l'ancienne coutume durant les #italic Kalendes#!.

Mes serviteurs ouvrent la porte, et les voix mélodieuses des jeunes gens emplissent nos oreilles. Une fois le chant terminé, mes serviteurs se tournent vers moi pour que je leur donne la permission d'offrir aux enfants des sucreries et de l'argent."

before: lesbos.0064.desc:0 "J'ai appris que certains de mes sujets avaient été capturés par des pirates. Pas "nos" pirates avec lesquels j'ai des connexions, évidemment, puisque nous avons des accords en place selon lesquels ils laissent mes territoires tranquilles.\n\nCependant, nos pirates alliés sont un atout précieux, car lorsque mon peuple m'a demandé de les aider à libérer leurs amis et leur famille capturés, nos pirates ont utilisé leurs réseaux pour m'aider à obtenir la libération de ces prisonniers - si je payais la rançon, bien entendu."
